JSON: Name: rift_linkage_subduction_polarity Title: Quantifying how pre-collisional rift linkage controls subduction polarity and mountain-belt evolution using 3D thermo-mechanical geodynamic models coupled to landscape evolution Short Hypothesis: For linked pre-collisional rift basins with a laterally homogeneous lithospheric strength field and no preferentially oriented mechanical weaknesses, basin offsets greater than 30 km cause inversion to develop opposite-polarity lithospheric subduction during continental collision, whereas offsets ≤30 km produce same-polarity subduction. Related Work: Prior studies used analogue sandbox experiments and 2D numerical cross-sections to show that extensional inheritance influences inversion tectonics and localisation of shortening; these indicated preferential reactivation of weak extensional structures and demonstrated that inherited faults affect thrust geometry. More recent 3D numerical efforts explored individual aspects of rift evolution or inversion but commonly neglected coupled mantle dynamics, the full 3D geometry of offset linked basins, or surface-process feedbacks. Existing approaches therefore (1) often treat only the brittle crust or 2D slices and omit lithospheric-scale mantle interactions; (2) do not systematically quantify the influence of along-strike basin offset and seed geometry on subduction polarity; (3) rarely include two-way coupling between deep geodynamics and landscape evolution; and (4) lack a simple force-balance diagnostic that predicts linkage thresholds and polarity selection. These gaps prevent a predictive mapping from observed topography/drainage patterns to deep lithospheric structure. Abstract: We address how the three-dimensional linkage geometry of pre-collisional rift basins controls inversion styles, subduction polarity selection, and the along-strike structure of collisional mountain belts. We propose a computational framework that couples high-resolution 3D thermo-mechanical geodynamic simulations of the crust and upper mantle with a landscape-evolution solver to capture two-way feedbacks between deep deformation and surface processes. The main contribution is a systematic parameter study across basin-offset, weak-seed geometry, and strength-contrast, together with a force-minimisation analysis that yields a quantitative offset threshold for linkage-driven polarity selection. Expected outcomes are (i) a reproducible threshold criterion (offset ≈ 30 km under homogeneous strength) separating same- and opposite-polarity inversion modes, (ii) diagnostics linking plan-view topography and drainage orientation to underlying subduction polarity, and (iii) a validated modelling suite applicable to natural cases such as the Pyrenees, Atlas and Greater Caucasus. The results provide a predictive template for interpreting orogen-scale 3D complexity from surface observables. Experiments: Datasets: 1) Synthetic model suite matching domain 1200 km × 600 km × 120 km with layered lithosphere (upper/mid crust 0–25 km, lower crust 25–35 km, lithospheric mantle to 120 km) and initial steady-state geotherm; 2) Natural DEMs and geophysical constraints for three test orogens: Pyrenees, Atlas, Greater Caucasus (ETOPO2/ETOPO1 or higher-resolution regional DEMs; available seismic tomography and gravity anomaly cross-sections). Baselines: A) 2D cross-section models with identical rheology but no mantle coupling; B) 3D models without two-way landscape coupling; C) published parameter set reproducing reference Model M1 (0 km offset). Parameter sweep: offset ∈ {0, 20, 50, 100, 150, 200, 300, 400} km; weak-seed geometries ∈ {rectangular notch, elongated angled seeds ±45°, varied dip}; strength-contrast factor f ∈ {1, 5, 10}; erosion coefficients K ∈ {1e-6, 5e-6, 1e-5 m0.2/yr}; post-rift cooling durations ∈ {0, 20, 50 Myr}. For each parameter combination run full 3D pTatin3D coupled to FastScape for model duration sufficient to reach mature orogen state (up to 63 Myr or until lateral boundary encounter). Output cadence: 0.5 Myr. Evaluation metrics: (1) Subduction polarity (categorical: same/opposite) determined from sign of integrated lithospheric mantle vertical motion and dip of dominant subducting slab; (2) Basin linkage (binary) using connectivity of inner-fault shearzones at seismogenic depths; (3) Offset threshold detection: logistic regression and change-point analysis to estimate offset value where probability(opposite polarity) crosses 50%; (4) Topographic metrics: along-strike elevation profiles, location and depth of transfer-zone low, correlation (Pearson r) between modeled and observed elevation swaths for natural cases; (5) Kinematic metrics: lateral translation distance of orogen centroid, cumulative crustal shortening, trapped mantle fragment volume; (6) Force metrics: compute depth-integrated lithospheric strength integrals and F_link vs F_direct as in force-minimisation analysis. Ablation studies: a) remove landscape coupling; b) disable strain weakening; c) introduce a preferentially oriented weakness field (vary orientation and strength) and re-run offset sweep to test hypothesis dependence on fabric. Resolution and sensitivity tests: double and half horizontal mesh resolution and vary strain-weakening threshold. Statistical tests: report fraction of runs yielding opposite polarity per offset bin, confidence intervals (95%) via bootstrapping, and sensitivity of threshold to rheological and surface-erosion parameters. Model-to-data comparison: for each natural case select model runs with closest along-strike topographic signature and compare predicted subduction polarity to independent geophysical indicators (seismic tomography, gravity anomalies) using confusion matrix and Cohen's kappa. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: results sensitive to rheological parameter choices (activation energies, pre-exponential factors, viscosity scaling) and to strain-weakening law and thresholds; mesh dependence arising from strain localisation and lack of regularisation may alter fault linkage behaviour. Data and evaluation biases: natural validation relies on imperfect seismic tomography and gravity interpretations that may ambiguously indicate subduction polarity; DEM-derived drainage diagnostics can be altered by post-collisional erosion or climatic signals leading to false correspondences. Scalability and compute limits: full 3D coupled runs at lithospheric scale with parameter sweeps are computationally expensive (hundreds to thousands of node-years), limiting ensemble size and resolution. Model simplifications limit generalization: constant along-strike erosion efficiency, omission of magmatism, melting, volatile-related weakening, and simplified post-rift cooling histories restrict applicability to systems where those processes are important; threshold values (e.g., 30 km) are parameter-dependent and not universal. Non-uniqueness: different combinations of offset, strength heterogeneity, and pre-existing fabric can produce similar surface observables, limiting deterministic inversion from topography alone.
